questions.title: Does the Minnesota Payment of Wages Act (MPWA) allow private employees to sue for 'average daily wage penalties' when the statute explicitly vests that enforcement power in the Commissioner?
questions.question_body: In *Cohen v. Consilio*, the court affirmed summary judgment against Cohen's MPWA claim because § 181.101(a) states that only the Commissioner can impose and collect penalties after serving a demand for payment. The court noted that while an employee can sue for back wages, they cannot sue for penalties unless the statute explicitly grants them that right (as seen in discharge/quit scenarios under §§ 181.13 and 181.14). I understand the statutory construction argument ('expressio unius'), but does this mean that even if an employer clearly violates the wage timing rules, a private plaintiff is completely barred from recovering statutory penalties under this specific section, regardless of the harm suffered? Is there any exception where a private suit for penalties is permitted under MPWA § 181.032 or elsewhere?

questions.title: Can a plaintiff maintain Article III standing to seek civil penalties payable to the state if their individual monetary damages (overtime and liquidated damages) have already been fully satisfied via settlement?
questions.question_body: The core of my confusion lies in Part II(B) of the opinion. Cohen stipulated he was paid all overtime and liquidated damages, leaving only civil penalties (payable to the Commissioner) disputed. The appellate court expressed concern about mootness/standing because Cohen lacks a direct financial stake in penalties paid to the government. However, citing *Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw*, civil penalties often serve as a deterrent against future violations, which theoretically gives a plaintiff standing even without personal monetary recovery. Why did the Eighth Circuit seem hesitant here compared to *Laidlaw*? Does the fact that these are Minnesota state law penalties rather than federal environmental fines change the standing analysis regarding 'redressability'?

questions.title: What is the legal standard for determining if a claim becomes 'voluntarily ceased' versus 'absolutely clear' that violations will not recur in a state labor law context?
questions.question_body: The court vacated and remanded the MFLSA penalty claim because it wasn't clear if Consilio's overtime policy was still in place or if it was just temporarily stopped during litigation. The opinion cites *City of Mesquite v. Aladdin's Castle* stating voluntary cessation doesn't automatically strip jurisdiction, but then asks if it is 'absolutely clear' behavior won't recur. How does a district court practically make this determination on remand? Do they look at internal corporate memos, public statements by management, or just whether the written policy document has been officially revoked? Since this is a class action context (even though it seems to have stalled), does the potential impact on other employees affect whether Cohen has standing to pursue these penalties?

questions.title: Did Cohen waive his MWTA claim regarding failure-to-notify penalties by failing to cite specific statutory authority in his appellate brief?
questions.question_body: Regarding Part II(C), Cohen argued Consilio violated the Minnesota Wage Theft Act (MWTA) by failing to provide notice of policy changes, yet he didn't point to any specific subsection granting him a right to civil penalties for this specific violation. The court dismissed this as waived under *Milligan*. My confusion is procedural: Did Cohen actually fail to identify *any* authority, or did he argue generally that 'penalties are available' without pinpointing the exact text? If he had cited § 181.032(d)(4) broadly claiming it allows penalties, would that have been sufficient to survive waiver, or was his failure to distinguish between 'wage recovery' and 'civil penalty recovery' fatal regardless of citation?

questions.title: Is an injunctive relief claim considered waived if raised for the first time in summary judgment briefing rather than through an amended complaint?
questions.question_body: In Part II(D), Cohen tried to shift his requested injunctive relief from his original complaint (which asked for specific orders) to asking simply for an order rescinding the illegal policy during summary judgment motions. The court said this new theory wasn't properly before them because Rule 15 requires amended complaints for new claims/theories. Isn't arguing that an existing policy must be rescinded just applying existing facts to existing law? Why isn't this treated as merely clarifying a prayer for relief based on undisputed facts rather than raising a brand new cause of action? What is the line between 'clarification' and 'new claim' in this context?

questions.title: How does Justice Kobes's concurrence suggest handling attorney's fees and prejudgment interest when liability itself is uncertain due to mootness concerns?
questions.question_body: Justice Kobes concurred specially noting she wasn't convinced Cohen had standing under *Laidlaw* but joined anyway because she agreed with vacating on mootness grounds. She also mentioned vacating rulings on attorney's fees and prejudgment interest without explaining why those were affected by her doubts about standing/mootness regarding penalties specifically. If a plaintiff loses standing on their primary claim (penalties), do ancillary claims like fees automatically fall too? Or was she suggesting that since we don't know if Cohen has standing at all, we can't award fees until jurisdiction is confirmed on remand?
